To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the accounting variables of firms in the United States are significantly more value-relevant than those of firms in Japan.

firms with different stakeholder-related reporting incentives have different value-relevance of their accounting variables, and this is true even when these firms face the identical institutional environment and accounting rules.
the earnings and book value of Japanese firms listed in U.S. markets are significantly more value-relevant than those for Japanese firms not listed on U.S. markets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of stakeholder-related incentives on the value-relevance and usefulness of accounting information.

the effects of stakeholder-related reporting incentives on the value-relevance characteristics of accounting information, and our findings suggest that these effects can be as strong as the effects of legal systems.
the effect of reporting incentives on the value-relevance and information content of accounting numbers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
accounting rules are not necessarily value-relevant in a country with code-law incentives.
accounting rules are only one factor that affects accounting value relevance.

the value-relevant characteristics of accounting information are affected not only by the country of origin of the accounting rules, but also by the legal and institutional environment in which a company operates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effect of the institutional environment on the value-relevance relationship is not only due to the accounting regime in the country of origin but also due to the reporting incentives created in the country of operation.
the value relevance of accounting variables depends on the reporting incentives that a firm faces and that these incentives are not necessarily determined by the accounting regime that a firm faces.

the accounting reports of the firms with different stakeholder-related reporting incentives have different value-relevance characteristics, even though they are based on the same set of accounting standards and the same set of financial statements.
The main takeaway from our work is that

accounting rules and the institutional environment are not the only determinants of the value-relevance properties of accounting variables, but that the reporting incentives created within a country's institutional environment are also critical.

, when examining the effects of accounting standards and reporting incentives globally, it is important to consider the reporting incentives created at all levels of the institutional environment, including the legal, political, economic, and social environment, and not just at a single level.

accounting standards and accounting reports should be considered within a broader context that includes the institutional and legal environment in which the firms are located and the incentives created by the reporting requirements of the firm's stakeholders.
